newsitem.title: UK: BADMINTON-SHUTTLECOCK ZOOMS TO WORLD RECORD 162 MPH.
newsitem.headline: BADMINTON-SHUTTLECOCK ZOOMS TO WORLD RECORD 162 MPH.

text.p: The racket may be lighter, the court shorter, and the object to smack not even round.
But badminton has sped ahead of arch rivals tennis and squash by proving that the oddly-shaped shuttlecock is faster than the fuzzy tennis ball and the compact rubber squash ball.

The shuttlecock is poised to enter the Guinness Book of Records at 162 miles per hour (261 kph) -- the speed it travels on the smash -- compared to squash's 151 mph (243 kph) and a mere 138 mph (222 kph) for tennis.
Badminton's promoters hope the speed record might bolster the sport's image and help move it out of other racket sports' shadows, particularly in regions where tennis and squash reign supreme.

"This shows it is quite an accomplished competitive sport. It is not a question of picking up a racket in the back garden and hitting about," said Mike Bowdich, technical expert at the International Badminton Federation in western England.
"The athletes are better prepared than tennis athletes. The advantage over tennis is that there are so many more elements. It requires a balance of finesse and power that tennis doesn't have."
Asked whether badminton's speed might woo people from tennis, Bowdich's counterpart at the International Tennis Federation in London, Andrew Cole, seemed sceptical.

"I don't know about that. They are very different games. They're talking about the smash -- that's just one stroke that doesn't take place that often whereas in tennis the serve takes place every point.
"But I have to admit I am a bit surprised. I never thought of the comparison, but it is a lightweight racket that can be swung faster."
When the shuttlecock is smashed it folds up on itself and compacts into a ball-like sphere, Bowdich explained, although he added that it rapidly loses speed as it travels through the air.
The speed record was set by British badminton Olympic team member Simon Archer last November, but has taken several months to be confirmed by record-keepers Guinness Publishing.
"A reply is going out shortly that it was accepted," said Amanda Brooks from Guinness.

It will be the first shuttlecock speed entry for badminton, but may not be the last. Once a new sports record hits the books, a deluge of aspiring entrants often contacts the company to inquire how to mount a challenge.
"A lot of people out there seem to think they can better new records," she said. "Sport always gets the most."
But Brian Littler, a badminton coach who attended the record-setting smash, cautioned that the feat would be difficult to beat.
"It takes technique and consistency, plus a good clean hit with plenty of power. No Joe Bloggs could beat this."
